+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: The Weight of Azra The transfer vessel hummed with the particular indifference of machinery that had no opinion about its cargo. Arthur Neegan sat in a bolted chair and watched the small display screen cycle through its diagnostics — pressure nominal, trajectory nominal, reactor output nominal — green text scrolling against grey steel with the bureaucratic patience of a system that had never once been asked what it thought about any of this. He found it oddly comforting. Somewhere between the third and fourth readout, he had decided that the screen was the most honest thing aboard. He had been given forty minutes to pack. The retinue — six of them, in the dove-grey uniforms of the Antares Diplomatic Corps, with the twin-star insignia pressed in silver at their shoulders — had waited outside his prefab with the particular politeness of men who are accustomed to not needing to ask twice. Their commander, a lean woman with close-cropped hair and the careful eyes of a surveyor, had handed him a document on a glass tablet. *Request for Consultation*, it read. *Voluntary.* He had looked at the six men behind her. "Of course," he had said. --- The vessel broke Martian orbit with a shudder that Arthur felt in his back teeth, and then the rust-coloured curve of the planet tilted away through the porthole and was replaced by the simple, absolute black of the transfer corridor between worlds. He had made this crossing twice before — once arriving, once returning briefly to settle his mother's estate on Callisto. Both times it had felt like erasure. The self you were on one world had no jurisdiction out here. A door slid open. The woman with the careful eyes entered and sat across from him without preamble. "Mr. Neegan. I'm Coordinator Vass. I apologise for the abruptness of the invitation." "You'll forgive me if I don't quite believe the apology." She almost smiled. "The party you're meeting asked me to convey that your cooperation is genuinely valued. That word — *genuinely* — was specified." "Who is the party?" "You'll have that answer in approximately four hours." She stood. "There's food in the forward compartment. The coffee is adequate." The door closed. The diagnostics screen cycled. *Trajectory nominal.* --- The station had no name on any chart Arthur had been given access to, which told him something. It occupied a gravitational null point between Mars and the belt — a location chosen, he suspected, less for convenience than for the elegant ambiguity of its jurisdiction. It was large enough to suggest permanence and spare enough to suggest that permanence had not been the original intention. He was shown through three corridors and two pressure doors and into a room that surprised him. It was warm. There were actual plants — small ones, in ceramic pots along a shelf — and the lighting was the amber of late afternoon rather than the surgical white of institutional spaces. A man sat at a round table with two cups already poured. He was perhaps sixty, with the broad, unhurried face of someone who had learned that patience was simply leverage applied slowly. "Mr. Neegan." He gestured to the chair opposite. "Please. The coffee here is better than adequate, whatever Vass told you." Arthur sat. He took the cup. The coffee was, in fact, excellent. "You have me at a disadvantage," Arthur said. "Temporarily." The man folded his hands on the table. "My name is Councillor Dresh. I represent certain interests within the Consolidated Outer Systems Assembly — which is to say, I represent the interests of approximately nine hundred million people who will, within the next decade, find themselves either protected or endangered by what sits underneath your mining plot on Mars." Arthur set down his cup. "That's a large number of people to attach to a survey claim." "It's a large deposit of Azra." Dresh's expression did not change. "Our geophysical models suggest you are sitting atop the largest single vein yet discovered. Forty times the yield of the Schiaparelli extraction site. Perhaps more." He paused to let that settle, the way a good engineer lets a structure bear its own weight before testing the joints. "You understand what that means for drive technology." "I understand what it means for weapons technology," Arthur said. "Yes." Dresh seemed to appreciate the correction. "Which is precisely why I wanted to speak with you before certain other parties did." He turned his cup slowly in its saucer. "The Terran Directorate has filed three separate legal challenges to your claim in the past eleven days. The Meridian Extraction Consortium has, we believe, retained two lobbyists and one less reputable type of operative. And the Antares Corps" — he glanced toward the door through which Coordinator Vass had presumably retreated — "is nominally neutral, which in practice means they are available to whoever makes the more persuasive argument." "And your argument?" Arthur asked. "Simple." Dresh looked at him directly for the first time. "Sign a development accord with the Assembly. We fund extraction, we control distribution, and we guarantee — legally, structurally, with teeth — that Azra from your vein does not enter the weapons market for a period of no less than thirty years. You receive a percentage that will make you, by any reasonable measure, extraordinarily wealthy. And nine hundred million people in the outer systems do not spend the next decade looking down the barrel of something that accelerates radioactive decay to weapons-grade output." The diagnostics screen on the wall cycled through its green text. *Pressure nominal. Reactor output nominal.* Arthur looked at the plants on the shelf. Someone had watered them recently. Someone had brought soil up from somewhere and decided that this cold, jurisdictionally ambiguous station needed something alive in it. "And if I decline?" he said. Dresh picked up his coffee. "Then someone less scrupulous than me will be having this conversation with you very shortly." He sipped. "And their coffee, I assure you, will be considerably worse."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the brief very well. It opens with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel as instructed, delivers the meeting with an unknown party (Councillor Dresh), keeps the scene primarily dialogue-driven with vivid scene-setting (the amber-lit room, the plants, the coffee motif), and sows intrigue via the Terran Directorate, Meridian Consortium, and Antares' "nominal neutrality." The Asimovian flavor is well captured: dialogue as intellectual chess, big-picture geopolitics delivered through small concrete details (coffee quality, watered plants, "Voluntary" in italics), and a coolly rational protagonist. The recurring diagnostics screen ("Trajectory nominal") is an effective motif. The ending line about coffee is a nice understated threat, very much in the classic mode. Weaknesses: the chapter is titled "Chapter Seven" though the story seems to be beginning—minor inconsistency. Some cleverness borders on preciousness ("the particular indifference of machinery that had no opinion about its cargo"; "patience was simply leverage applied slowly")—a touch more ornamental than Asimov's plain style, though not purple. Dresh is somewhat stock (the urbane, patient spymaster), and Arthur's characterization is thin—he's mostly a reactive listener. The stakes are told more than dramatized, and the offer arrives without much genuine menace or tension. Still, the prose is clean, dialogue crisp, and pacing tight at ~1000 words. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations The red light makes everyone look like they're confessing something. I've thought about that before, in other darkrooms, other semesters. But tonight it feels specifically true, specifically aimed at the boy standing three feet away from me, watching a photograph materialize in the developer tray like he's witnessing something sacred. Which, I suppose, he is. That's the thing about Elliot. He treats ordinary moments like they deserve reverence. He's humming. Something soft and tuneless, or almost tuneless—there's a shape to it that keeps almost becoming a real song and then dissolving. His fingers hover at the edge of the tray without touching the chemical bath, and the red light catches the silver ring on his thumb, the smudged liner he always wears slightly imprecise, like he applied it in low light or applied it deliberately imprecise. I've never been able to tell which. I've been cataloguing him for four months. That's the honest version of what I've been doing. I'm not proud of the cataloguing, exactly. It's not my most dignified impulse. But Elliot arrived in Experimental Photography in September wearing a shredded fishnet top over a long-sleeve thermal and carrying a camera bag held together with electrical tape and band patches, and something in my brain just—flagged him. Filed him under *pay attention to this one.* I'm twenty-five. I've been in this program long enough to know which students are interesting and which students are performing interesting. Elliot was the real thing. Quiet in a way that had weight to it. "It's coming," he says, and his voice has that quality it always has, like he's slightly surprised by good things. The image is one of his—a double exposure, two negatives sandwiched. A hand holding a flower, overlaid with the same hand holding nothing. The emptiness and the fullness occupying the same space. It's his whole thesis in one frame, honestly, though he hasn't said that out loud yet. "It's good," I say. And then, because I'm me and I can't help it: "The registration is perfect. How did you get the alignment that precise?" "Luck, mostly." He glances at me sideways. "And I did it like six times." I smile. I'm standing close enough to smell the faint chemical sharpness of the developer on his hands, underneath something warmer. I've been managing my proximity to Elliot all semester with what I consider impressive discipline. He goes back to humming. The thing is, I have a type. I've always had a type, and I've always been clear about it, which is something I pride myself on. I like defined edges. I like people who know what they are. I've dated women who were very specifically women, men who were very specifically men, and I've liked the clarity of that, the way desire had clean lines I could follow. I'm a person who takes charge. I need to know the territory I'm navigating. Elliot is not clear edges. Elliot is a double exposure. And I have been quietly, inconveniently losing my mind about him since October. "Can I ask you something?" he says. "Yeah." He doesn't ask it immediately. He uses the tongs to lift the print, move it to the stop bath, and I watch his hands work with the careful attention he gives everything. The humming stops. "Do you ever feel like—" He pauses. Starts again. "Like you've been performing a version of yourself for so long that you can't tell anymore if you're performing or if that's actually you?" The question lands somewhere specific in my chest. I think about the version of Dani I've been performing in this darkroom for four months—the one who is casually interested, professionally collegial, definitely not cataloguing. "Yeah," I say. "I know that feeling." He nods slowly. The print moves to the fix bath. "I've been thinking a lot about—" Another pause, longer. The red light makes his face look like something being developed too. Like he's in the process of becoming visible. "About gender stuff. My gender stuff. I don't know if I'm—I don't know what I am, exactly. I've been trying on different words and none of them fit perfectly and some of them fit *mostly* and I just." He exhales. "I don't know why I'm telling you this." "Because it's a confessional in here," I say. "The red light." He looks at me then, really looks, and something in his expression does something complicated to my composure. "Yeah," he says quietly. "Maybe." I want to ask questions. I want to take charge of this conversation, map it, understand exactly where he is and what he needs and how to respond correctly. That's my instinct. Take the territory, know the terrain. But I can feel that instinct as the wrong one, feel it the way you feel a wrong note. This is not my territory to take. "That sounds like important work," I say instead. "The trying on." "It's exhausting." "I bet." "Does it—" He stops. Looks at the print in the fix bath. "Does it change anything? For you. About working together." The question is careful. Tentative in a way that makes me understand he's braced for something. I think about what answer he's braced for, and it makes something in me go protective and fierce and tender all at once, which is a combination I don't have a lot of experience with. "No," I say. And then, because honesty seems to be what this red light demands: "It makes me more interested in your work, actually. Which I didn't think was possible." He's quiet for a moment. "Just my work?" he says, and there's something in it—not quite teasing, not quite serious. Something in between, something new. The photograph floats in the chemical bath. A hand holding everything and nothing simultaneously. "We should get the print to the wash," I say. But I'm smiling, and he can see it, and the red light holds us both in its slow, developing patience.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of quiet, atmospheric writing. The darkroom setting is used effectively as both literal space and metaphor—the developing photograph mirrors Elliot's developing selfhood, and the red light as "confessional" is established early and paid off naturally. Dani's voice is consistent: wry, self-aware, slightly self-deprecating about her own "cataloguing," with a clear assertive personality that the prose itself enacts in its confident rhythms. The central tension—Dani's take-charge instinct colliding with her recognition that "this is not my territory to take"—is handled with genuine nuance. The piece resists easy resolution: Elliot's disclosure is halting and realistic, Dani's response is measured, and the ending lands on ambiguity ("Just my work?") rather than a tidy romantic payoff. The double-exposure image (hand holding a flower / hand holding nothing) is a well-chosen symbolic anchor without being overworked. Minor weaknesses: the piece is somewhat short of the requested 1000 words (roughly 850), and some of Dani's introspective passages ("I've been cataloguing him for four months") edge toward telling rather than showing, though the confessional first-person mode partially justifies this. A few lines ("something in his expression does something complicated to my composure") are slightly vague in a way that feels like a dodge rather than precision. The "performing a version of yourself" exchange is a touch on-the-nose as thematic statement. The chemistry is present but understated—appropriate, though some readers may want more concrete interaction to earn the "unexpected chemistry" beat. Overall: polished, controlled, emotionally intelligent work with small imperfections in specificity and length. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma The Trevi Fountain announced itself before Ben Hartley ever saw it — a roar of cascading water cutting through the mid-morning heat, tourists packed three-deep along the marble railing, coins glinting in the basin like scattered promises. Ben stood precisely four metres from the kerb, nose buried in his guidebook, mouthing the Latin inscription above Neptune's head with the quiet concentration of a man who had mistaken thoroughness for experience. He never heard the motorcycle. The Vespa shrieked past so close that the wing mirror clipped his guidebook clean from his hands, sending it spinning into a puddle of tourist-spilled gelato. Ben stumbled backwards into a Japanese couple, apologised to them in French, then apologised again in English, then simply held up both hands in a gesture of universal mortification. "*Cretino!*" The rider had stopped. She swung off the Vespa with the fluid economy of someone who had never once in her life been uncertain of her body, yanking off her helmet to reveal dark hair, darker eyes, and an expression that suggested she was deciding whether to be furious or entertained. "You were standing in the road," she said, switching to English with the casual authority of someone who speaks four languages and is proud of none of them. "I was on the pavement," Ben said. "The *pavement*." She looked down at his feet. He was, in fact, standing in the road. "Ah." "I may have drifted slightly." "You drift like a ship." She retrieved his guidebook from the gelato puddle, held it between two fingers as though it were evidence. "*Roma per Principianti.*" She looked up. "Rome for Beginners." "It's research," Ben said. "I'm an academic." "Of course you are." She handed it back. Her name, she told him without being asked, was Alessandra. She said it the way Romans say everything — as though the word itself were a small, beautiful fact about the universe. --- He should have walked away. He knew that. Instead he found himself accepting a coffee at a bar so narrow two people couldn't pass without turning sideways, watching Alessandra drink her espresso standing up, the way Romans do, the cup gone in two practiced sips. "What do you study?" she asked. "Classical architecture. The persistence of ancient form in modern urban space." She stared at him. "So you look at buildings." "Essentially, yes." "I deliver things between buildings." She set down her cup. "We are not so different." Ben laughed — a surprised, genuine laugh that seemed to startle them both slightly. Alessandra's mouth curved. She was watching him the way a cat watches something it hasn't decided whether to play with or ignore. He noticed, without quite processing it, that when they left the bar, the ceramic espresso spoon had disappeared from his saucer and reappeared, somehow, in the breast pocket of her jacket. --- "I will show you Rome," she announced outside, straddling the Vespa. "I have a lecture to prepare," Ben said. "Get on." He got on. She drove the way she apparently did everything — with complete disregard for conventional boundaries. She took him through the Trastevere backstreets, past laundry strung between buildings like festival bunting, past a *trattoria* where an old man was arguing passionately with a cat. She stopped at a gate in a garden wall, produced a key that Ben was fairly certain she hadn't possessed ten minutes ago, and led him through to a private courtyard where orange trees grew in terracotta pots and the city noise dropped away like a coat slipping from your shoulders. "This is someone's property," Ben said. "It is *everyone's* property," Alessandra said, lying back on a stone bench and closing her eyes. "That is the correct Roman philosophy." "That is not the correct Roman philosophy." "Ben." She said his name for the first time. It sounded different in her mouth — shorter, more definite, like a full stop. "Sit down." He sat down. --- They were crossing the Campo de' Fiori when a man called out her name. He was perhaps fifty, barrel-chested, with the weathered look of someone who had spent decades outdoors and several of those decades regretting specific decisions. "*Alessandra, figlia del diavolo.*" "*Tonio,*" she said warmly, kissing both his cheeks. Tonio looked at Ben with the frank assessment of a man evaluating livestock. "English?" "British, yes. Ben Hartley." "You know this woman how long?" "About three hours." Tonio nodded slowly, as though this confirmed something he had long suspected about the British. He leaned toward Ben with the gravity of a man delivering scripture. "She took my grandfather's watch," he said. "Nineteen ninety-eight. We did not find it for six years. It was in the lining of her school bag." He paused. "She was eleven." Ben looked at Alessandra. "I was returning it," she said serenely. "*For six years?*" "It took time to find the right moment." Tonio gripped Ben's arm. "Go to your hotel," he said. "Read your books. Eat pasta. Go home." He released him, kissed Alessandra on both cheeks again with the helpless affection of someone who has long since surrendered to a force of nature, and disappeared into the crowd. Ben turned to Alessandra. She was already walking, hands in her jacket pockets, the afternoon light catching the angles of her face. "Should I be concerned?" he asked, falling into step beside her. "Everyone should be a little concerned," she said. "It keeps you alert." --- They ate at a table outside a restaurant that Alessandra had chosen by the method of walking in, inspecting the kitchen without invitation, and declaring it acceptable. The owner had not objected. Ben was beginning to understand that very few people objected to Alessandra, not because she was intimidating, but because her certainty was somehow more contagious than any argument against it. The wine was cold. The evening was warm. Rome turned amber around them. "You'll go back tomorrow," she said. It wasn't a question. "To my flat, yes. I'm here for three months." She looked at him over her glass with an expression he couldn't parse — something between calculation and something softer, which she seemed to notice and promptly set aside. "Three months," she repeated. "Plenty of time," Ben said, and surprised himself by meaning it. Alessandra smiled — not the sharp, testing smile of the morning, but something quieter, which she hid quickly behind her wine glass, as though she hadn't quite intended to let him see it. Outside, a scooter alarm was going off. Neither of them mentioned that it might be hers.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, confident piece of commercial fiction. The prose is crisp and witty, with a strong comic voice — lines like "apologised to them in French, then apologised again in English" and Tonio's "She was eleven" beat land well. The scene structure (fragmented day-in-Rome vignettes) matches the prompt's request for interconnected short scenes. Alessandra's kleptomania is handled with exactly the requested subtlety: the espresso spoon, the mysterious key, the scooter alarm at the end. Ben's polite fluster is consistent and believable. The Tonio scene is the highlight — it delivers exposition of her character through a third party with humor rather than telling. Weaknesses: the word count falls short of 1000 (roughly 850), and the prompt's "" placeholder was left unfilled/ignored. The "spark" of romance is present but somewhat thin — the prompt asked for escalating outlandish situations and a culminating payoff at parting; the piece ends on a wry note rather than a real culmination, and the day's escalation (courtyard trespass) is fairly mild. Some jokes are slightly familiar (cat-arguing trattoria, "everyone's property"). Alessandra occasionally tips into stock "fiery Italian woman" archetype, though Tonio's scene complicates it nicely. The prose occasionally over-reaches ("like scattered promises," "a coat slipping from your shoulders") but stays controlled. Overall: highly readable, funny, well-structured, with minor instruction shortfalls and a slightly underpowered climax. Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. # The Last Outpost — Chapter One: Dreads Askew The thing about asteroid belt evenings is that they don't really exist. No sun to set, no sky to bruise purple and orange. But we invented our own version here at the Outpost — Davo dims the overhead panels to about sixty percent around the nineteenth hour, and something in the human and near-human brain just *accepts* it. Evening. Here we go. I'm pulling a second pour for Mick Oradeen, a silicate miner with hands like geology, when the stranger comes in. I notice the dreads first. They're the kind that move on their own — bioluminescent tentacle-locs, probably gene-modded, probably expensive once upon a time — and right now they're doing that anxious writhing thing, coiling and recoiling against each other like they can't agree on a direction. The stranger is humanoid, slight, wearing a jacket that's seen three too many pressure-seal failures. They navigate the crowd without looking at it, which takes a particular kind of practice, and they find the far end of the bar the way a stone finds the bottom of a well. Quiet. Fast. Inevitable. "Vega whisky, neat." A pause. The dreads knot briefly around each other. "Better make that a double." I already have the bottle out. That's not intuition — that's just bartending. "Vega's a good choice," I say, setting the glass down and pouring two fingers, then two more. "Means you've either had a very good day or a very bad one." "Does anyone order Vega whisky after a good day?" "Honestly? No." I leave the bottle nearby, which is either generosity or professional pessimism, and I start wiping the section of bar between us. It's already clean. It's always already clean. But my hands need something to do when my ears are working this hard. The stranger drinks. Not desperately — carefully, like the whisky is information they're processing. The dreads settle by maybe ten percent. Around us, the Outpost does its evening thing. Mick Oradeen has found someone to argue with about silicate yields. The Pellucid Sisters — three merchant women who share a ship and apparently a single collective opinion about everything — are debating something in their layered harmonic language over by the viewport. Farther back, in the booth I privately call the Confessional, two people who are definitely not supposed to be meeting are definitely meeting. Normal. All of it beautifully, boringly normal. "You work here long?" the stranger asks. "Long enough that I stopped counting," I say. "Nets." "Sorry?" "My name. Nets." The dreads do something that might be a nod. "Sable." "Just passing through, Sable, or are you docking a while?" Another careful sip. "That depends." I wipe the same spot. "On?" "On whether a thing I'm looking for is actually here." Sable sets the glass down and looks at me directly for the first time. Their eyes are interesting — irises with that fractured amber quality that usually means Kepler-heritage, three or four generations back. "I was told the Outpost keeps records. Transaction logs. Cargo manifests going back, what — fifteen years?" "Davo keeps records," I say. "Davo keeps *everything*. It's either his greatest virtue or his most alarming quality, depending on the day." "Can I talk to Davo?" "You're talking to me first." I say it pleasantly, but I say it. Sable seems to understand the structure of this, because they don't push. "Fair," they say. I pour them a small, unsolicited top-up, which is my version of *keep going*. "I'm looking for a cargo shipment," Sable says. "Registered under a shell company — Auric Meridian Holdings. It would have come through here about eight years ago, maybe nine. Biological material, listed on the manifest as agricultural samples." They say *agricultural samples* the way you'd say *that's not blood, it's paint*. "I have reason to believe the listing was fraudulent." "Biological material gets flagged," I say carefully. "Customs runs a secondary scan on anything organic." "I know." Sable's jaw tightens. The dreads do a slow, unhappy spiral. "Which means either customs cleared it legitimately, or customs was—" They stop. "Helped along," I offer. "Yes." I keep wiping. The spot is practically a philosophical concept at this point, a meditation on cleanliness. I'm thinking about eight years ago, which is two years before I arrived here, which should mean this has nothing to do with me, which is the kind of logic that has historically preceded things having everything to do with me. "What kind of biological material?" I ask. Sable looks at their glass. "People," they say quietly. "Children, specifically. Eleven of them. They were mine to protect, and someone moved them through a legitimate cargo hub in a fraudulent shipment, and I have spent—" Their voice does something complicated and then rights itself. "I have spent a long time following a very cold trail to this particular rock." The Outpost hums around us. Mick Oradeen laughs his gravel laugh. The Pellucid Sisters harmonize briefly in disagreement. "I need those records," Sable says. "And I need to know if anyone here remembers that shipment. Someone always remembers something." They're right about that. That's the thing about a place like this — it's a hub, which means it's a memory. Eight years of miners and merchants and people passing through, and the Outpost absorbed all of it, the way stone absorbs heat. The trouble is, I know who keeps the oldest memories here. The ones that predate the official logs. And I know why asking him is going to be complicated. I set down my rag. Pick it up again. "Davo," I say finally, "closes his records office at twenty-two hundred." Sable glances at the clock panel above the bottles. "That's twenty minutes." "Then you should probably finish that drink," I say, "and I should probably figure out how to explain to my boss why I'm bringing a stranger into his records office after hours." I pause. "He doesn't like strangers." Sable looks at me. "But you're going to help me." I pick up the rag again. "I haven't decided yet," I say, which is a lie, and probably both of us know it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of cozy sci-fi that hits nearly all of the prompt's requirements with confidence and craft. The first-person present-tense voice of Nets is consistent, wry, and economical — the "wiping the clean bar" motif is a well-executed recurring beat that shows rather than tells her nervous attentiveness. The dialogue-to-narration ratio lands close to the requested 60%, and the chapter establishes a clear conflict (Sable's search for records of a trafficked shipment of children) without resolving it, as instructed. Strengths: The worldbuilding is delivered through casual, lived-in detail (Davo's dimming panels, the Pellucid Sisters' harmonic speech, the "Confessional" booth) rather than exposition dumps. Sable's revelation about the children is genuinely affecting and earns the chapter's tonal shift from cozy to tense. The ending — "I haven't decided yet, which is a lie" — is a well-turned beat that promises continuation without false resolution. Nets's internal logic ("the kind of logic that has historically preceded things having everything to do with me") plants her own connection to the mystery with a light touch. Weaknesses: Some of the banter is a touch familiar — the "good day or bad day" whisky exchange is stock bartender dialogue, and the "bioluminescent tentacle-locs" stranger-with-a-mysterious-past is a well-worn archetype. The "agricultural samples" reveal of trafficked children edges toward a melodramatic stakes-escalation that cozy sci-fi usually handles more obliquely, though the restrained delivery mostly mitigates this. A few metaphors ("hands like geology," "the way a stone finds the bottom of a well") are effective, but the piece occasionally leans on its own cleverness ("a meditation on cleanliness"). The prose is polished but not quite virtuosic; it's professional, controlled, and pleasant rather than revelatory. Overall, this is a competent, engaging chapter with a distinct voice, well-managed pacing, and a satisfying hook. It doesn't quite reach the level of a masterpiece, but it avoids nearly all the common failure modes. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gone South ## Chapter One: The City That Care Forgot The strap slides off my shoulder again. I hitch it back up and keep walking, like I know where I'm going, like I have a single solitary plan beyond *not Tennessee*. The air here is a living thing — thick and green-smelling and hot in a way that's completely different from home. Home hot is dry and mean. This hot is *wet*. It wraps around you like it's trying to tell you something. It's eight in the morning and New Orleans is already awake and already strange. Marcus, the truck driver who'd picked me up outside of Memphis, had been decent enough. Didn't ask too many questions. Dropped me at a gas station on the edge of the French Quarter with a twenty-dollar bill and something that was almost an apology in his eyes. "End of my route, kid," was all he said. I'd watched his taillights disappear and felt the specific terror of having actually done the thing you planned to do. The strap slips again. *Fix the damn strap, Taylor.* I stop outside a bakery. Through the window I can see a woman arranging pastries in a glass case, moving them with the focused tenderness of someone handling small animals. My stomach makes a sound like a dying engine. I haven't eaten since a gas station hot dog somewhere in Mississippi, which felt disgusting going down and feels worse in retrospect. I have forty-three dollars. The twenty from Marcus, plus twenty-three of my own. I do the math the way you do when you're trying not to panic: forty-three dollars, no phone service because Mom pays that bill and I am *not* calling Mom, no ID that reflects anything true about me, and a backpack containing: two changes of clothes, a journal, a phone charger, my sketchbook, and a photograph I almost left behind but didn't. I didn't leave it behind. I keep walking. --- By ten o'clock I've established several facts about the French Quarter. One: it smells like beer even when it's not serving beer yet. Two: the buildings are genuinely beautiful in a crumbling, complicated way, all iron lacework and peeling paint, like they're gorgeous and they know it and they're tired of trying. Three: I fit here approximately zero percent. Everyone seems to know the rhythm of this place and I don't know the first beat. I find a bench in a small square — Jackson Square, a sign says — and sit down hard. A man nearby is playing saxophone, something slow and liquid, and pigeons are doing their stupid pigeon business around his feet. I pull out my sketchbook because it's the one thing I know how to do when my brain gets too loud. The too-loud thing it keeps doing is replaying Dad's face. Not the anger. The anger I'd prepared for, sort of. It was the *confusion* that broke something in me — that specific look of a person encountering a word they don't have a definition for. Like I'd walked into the kitchen and announced I was a different species. *I don't understand what you're telling me*, he'd said. *I know*, I'd said. *I know you don't.* I'm drawing the bakery woman from memory — the careful way she moved — when a voice says, "That's pretty good." I look up. The person standing there is maybe my age, maybe a year older, with close-cropped hair and a nose ring and the particular quality of stillness that belongs to people who've learned to take up as little space as possible. They're wearing a flannel shirt in this heat, sleeves down, which is a choice that registers somewhere in the back of my mind. "Sorry," they say, not sounding sorry. "I'm Reyna." "Taylor." Reyna sits down on the other end of the bench with the casual confidence of someone who does this all the time, and I realize with a slow cold certainty that they probably do. There's a backpack at their feet too. Older than mine. More defeated-looking. "You got that brand-new runaway energy," Reyna says, not unkindly. "It wears off." "I'm not—" I start. Reyna raises one eyebrow. "Okay," I say. "Yeah." "How long?" "Since last night." Something moves across Reyna's face. Not pity exactly. Recognition, maybe. "You eat?" "Not really." "Come on then." They stand up, sling the beaten-up backpack over one shoulder. "There's a place on Decatur that does biscuits. Woman who runs it doesn't ask questions." I should not follow a stranger. I know this. I have been told this my entire life by people who were, at that exact moment, the main danger in my life. I look at Reyna — at the careful stillness, the sleeves-down flannel, the way they're not quite making eye contact, like they're offering something and trying not to look like they're offering it — and I make a judgment call. I stand up. The strap slides off my shoulder. "Your buckle's broken," Reyna says. "I know." "I've got a safety pin somewhere." We walk. The saxophone follows us for half a block then fades into the general music of the city, which has its own bass note running under everything, some frequency I can feel in my sternum. I think about the photograph in my bag. Me and my cousin Deb, two summers ago, both of us laughing at something off-camera. I look happy in it. I look like a person who doesn't know yet what they are. I know now. That's the thing nobody tells you about finally saying the true thing out loud: even when it burns everything down, even when you're two states away with forty-three dollars and a broken strap and no plan — You still know. And knowing is not nothing. Reyna stops outside a narrow doorway and looks back at me. "You coming?" "Yeah," I say. "I'm coming."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, controlled piece of YA first-person narration. The voice is consistent and distinctive — wry, defensive, self-aware, with a rhythmic use of short sentences and italics for internal emphasis that feels authentic to a smart, wounded 16-year-old. The mixed tense requested by the prompt is handled naturally (past tense for backstory, present for the unfolding day). Adherence to instructions is excellent: Taylor arrives in New Orleans, spends their first day there, meets Reyna (a fellow runaway with implied secrets — the sleeves-down flannel in heat is a nicely understated hint of self-harm or concealment), navigates uncertainty about trust, and the internal monologue is threaded throughout with genuine conflict (fear vs. hunger, caution vs. loneliness, grief vs. the relief of self-knowledge). The word count lands near the seed. Strengths: the imagery is specific and fresh without being purple ("home hot is dry and mean. This hot is wet"); the father flashback is economical and devastating ("I don't understand what you're telling me" — the confusion rather than the anger as the wound is a sharp, non-obvious choice); the recurring broken strap works as a motif; the ending lands on earned, tentative hope rather than false resolution. The line "I have been told this my entire life by people who were, at that exact moment, the main danger in my life" is a standout — dark, funny, and true. Minor weaknesses: Reyna is somewhat stock — the wise, world-weary street kid dispensing cryptic guidance is a familiar archetype, and their dialogue ("You got that brand-new runaway energy... It wears off") flirts with quirk-by-numbers. The biscuit-shop woman "who doesn't ask questions" is a cliché of the genre. The piece stops just as the real story begins, so the "issues and secrets" of the fellow runaway are only gestured at, not developed. A few aphorisms ("knowing is not nothing") edge toward tidy. The ending's uplift is mild and earned, but the final beat is slightly neat. Still, the prose flows naturally, the emotional complexity is real, and nothing feels amateurish or overwrought. This is confident, publishable-grade YA writing. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 77.0
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The thing about Chewy was that he had survived the collapse in better shape than most humans, which said something either very complimentary about animatronic stuffed koalas or very uncomplimentary about humans, depending on your philosophical disposition. Midas had found him in the ruins of what the faded signage suggested had once been a "Family Entertainment Megaplex," which was either a place where families went to be entertained on a mega scale or some kind of pre-collapse religious institution. The distinction, at this point, was largely academic. Chewy's fur had gone the colour of old dishwater. One glass eye was slightly more optimistic than the other, perpetually aimed skyward as though expecting better weather. Every forty-seven minutes, with the mechanical reliability that had outlasted civilization itself, he emitted a fragment of whatever advertising gospel had been encoded into his small grey chest. "Right," said Midas, spreading the hand-drawn map across the bonnet of the dead car they used as a planning table. "The granary." "*Taste the rainbow,*" said Chewy. "The granary," Midas repeated, in the tone of a man who had learned to absorb non-sequiturs the way deserts absorb rain—completely and without visible effect. "Betterman says there's three months of grain in there, possibly four if we're not greedy, which we won't be because we're practically saints." Chewy regarded the map with his asymmetric gaze. The granary was, by Midas's reckoning, approximately four kilometres northeast, past the collapsed overpass, through the market district where Geraldine Muck operated her informal toll system, and around the edge of what everyone now called the Smelly Part, for reasons that rewarded neither investigation nor explanation. The plan was elegant in its simplicity. Walk there. Get grain. Walk back. Midas had constructed this plan over two days, which was two days more than he usually spent on plans, and he felt justifiably proud of it. He had not accounted for the goat. --- The goat appeared approximately eleven minutes into the journey, at the point where the road curved past the old pharmacy. It was a large goat, the colour of bad intentions, with the eyes of something that had made peace with chaos and found the arrangement agreeable. It was standing in the middle of the road eating what appeared to be someone's boot. "We go around," said Midas. The goat looked at him. "We definitely go around," said Midas, going around. The goat followed. It continued to follow them through the market district, which complicated the negotiation with Geraldine Muck considerably, as Geraldine had a longstanding and loudly expressed position on goats, their character, their ancestry, and their fundamental unsuitability for civil society. The toll, which had begun as two tins of preserved peaches, escalated through a series of goat-related grievances to four tins, a length of copper wire, and a formal written apology for the goat's behaviour, which Midas composed on the spot with the resigned fluency of a man who had written many apologies for things that were not, strictly speaking, his fault. "*You're worth it,*" said Chewy, from under Midas's arm. "Thank you," said Geraldine, unexpectedly mollified. --- The granary, when they reached it, was locked. This was not surprising. What was surprising was that it was locked from the inside, which suggested either tremendous foresight on the part of whoever had locked it, or that someone was currently inside, which proved, upon closer inspection, to be exactly the case. "There's someone in there," said Midas. The goat attempted to eat the door. The someone in there turned out to be three someones: a pair of brothers named Ott and Ott (they were, they explained without apparent embarrassment, both named Ott, following a clerical error at birth that had never been corrected and had eventually achieved the status of tradition), and a woman named Priscilla who had locked herself in three weeks ago following a dispute about turnips that had, in the telling, achieved an almost mythological complexity. They were not, technically, hostile. They were, however, not inclined to share, which amounted to the same practical outcome. Negotiations lasted forty minutes. Chewy contributed "*New formula, same great taste*" at the thirty-two minute mark, which broke the tension sufficiently that Priscilla laughed, and laughing Priscilla was, it emerged, a substantially more reasonable Priscilla than non-laughing Priscilla. They left with one sack of grain. It was not three months' worth. It was not four months' worth. It was, Midas calculated, walking back through the market district with the goat still in attendance, approximately eleven days' worth if everyone was careful and nobody had seconds. He chose to regard this as a partial success. Partial successes were, in his experience, the primary currency of the post-collapse world, and he had developed a connoisseur's appreciation for them. --- They made it back to the Smelly Part before the rain started, and through the Smelly Part before Midas's left boot sole finally surrendered its long argument with structural integrity, and past the old pharmacy before the goat, apparently satisfied that it had discharged some obscure goatly obligation, departed without ceremony into a side street and was gone. Home base was a former insurance office, which Midas found appropriate in ways he couldn't entirely articulate. He set the grain in the corner, hung his wet coat on the filing cabinet, and lowered himself into the salvaged armchair with the careful deliberateness of a man whose body had begun submitting formal complaints. Chewy sat on the desk, one eye skyward, one eye watching the door. Forty-seven minutes after they'd arrived home, right on schedule, he said: "*Because you deserve the very best.*" Midas looked at the single sack of grain. At his bootless foot. At the map, which had gotten wet and was now largely fictional. "Sure," he said. "Absolutely." Outside, it continued to rain, which was at least consistent.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that captures Pratchett's dry asides, footnote-style digressions, and affectionate absurdism. The structure follows the prompt precisely: deliberation over the day's mission (the granary), the mission going sideways (goat, Geraldine Muck's toll escalation, locked granary, the Ots and Priscilla), and a return home that is worse for wear in multiple ways (one sack instead of three months, ruined boot, wet fictional map, body aches). The word count lands near 1000. Strengths: Chewy's advertising-jingle non-sequiturs are a genuinely clever running gag, and the payoff — "Because you deserve the very best" landing on Midas's pile of partial failures — is well-timed and bittersweet. The goat is a classic Pratchett-style agent of chaos, and the toll negotiation with its escalating written apology is the comic highlight. The prose is controlled, with good rhythm and several excellent lines ("the colour of bad intentions," "partial successes were... the primary currency of the post-collapse world"). The insurance-office home base is a nice ironic touch. Weaknesses: The plot is thin and the granary occupants (Ott and Ott, Priscilla) are one-joke characters who resolve too easily — Chewy's slogan breaking the tension is convenient and slightly unearned. The turnip dispute is referenced but never made vivid, a missed opportunity. The ending, while tonally right, is a bit pat; the emotional register stays safely in wry and never risks anything deeper. Some jokes (the Smelly Part) are Pratchett-derivative rather than fresh. Dialogue is functional but Midas's voice and Chewy's are the only distinct ones. Overall this is confident, polished, and faithful to the brief, if not transcendent. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 88.0
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Wrong Kind of Quiet The bell above the door didn't so much ring as wheeze, and Maddox Cole — who had, in the last calendar year, graced the covers of *Empire*, *GQ*, and the front page of the *Daily Mail* three times — stumbled into Penmorfa Books looking like a man who had just been chased by wolves. He had been chased by something worse. "Shut the door," he said, to no one in particular, then shut it himself and pressed his back against it. Through the rain-blurred glass, two figures with cameras jogged past without stopping. He exhaled. "We're open, by the way," said a voice. "In case you were wondering. No need to ask." He turned. Behind the counter, a woman was looking at him over the top of a hardback, with the particular expression of someone who had been enjoying five minutes of peace and was conducting a calm audit of exactly how much it had been disturbed. She had dark hair escaping from a knot, ink on her left index finger, and the air of a person who was not, even slightly, impressed. "Sorry," Maddox said. He smiled. It was the smile — the one that had made a film critic in Los Angeles describe him as *'disarmingly, almost unfairly attractive.'* "Bit of a situation outside." "Mm." She turned a page. He looked around the shop. It was narrow and warm, crammed floor to ceiling with books in a way that suggested organisation had been attempted and then affectionately abandoned. Rain tapped at the window. Somewhere, a radiator ticked. "You're not going to ask what kind of situation?" "Not particularly, no." Maddox blinked. He drifted toward the counter with the practiced ease of a man who had learned, very young, that moving toward people usually worked in his favour. "I'm Maddox Cole." "I know who you are." She didn't look up. "You're blocking the Welsh Poetry section." He stepped aside. "You recognised me." "You're very tall and you've been in several films. It's not detective work." She finally lowered the book. Her eyes were sharp and brown and thoroughly unimpressed. "I'm Rhiannon. This is my shop. Are you going to buy something, or are you just using it as a bunker?" "Both, potentially." He leaned an elbow on the counter. "What are you reading?" She held up the cover. *The Complete Works of R.S. Thomas.* Something shifted in his expression — not the performance of interest, but the real thing, arriving uninvited. "Seriously?" "Why *seriously?*" "I've been trying to get through *Pietà* for three weeks. It keeps stopping me dead. I get four lines in and I have to put it down." Rhiannon was quiet for a moment. She set the book on the counter. "Which four lines?" He straightened, and for the first time since entering the shop, looked slightly uncertain. "*I have nowhere to go. The hand I put out / to feel the pulse of the wind / encounters nothing—*" He stopped. "Then I just sit there feeling a bit bleak." "That's the correct response," she said. Something in her voice had changed — not warmer, exactly, but less armoured. "Most people find him too austere." "Most people haven't spent a lot of time alone on film sets at three in the morning." "Is that where you read poetry? Film sets?" "Is that strange?" "It's not what I pictured." "What did you picture?" She picked up her book again, but he noticed she didn't open it. "Someone reading scripts, mostly. Possibly looking at himself in mirrors." Maddox laughed — a real one, shorter and less polished than his usual. "I do that *after* the poetry." He glanced along the shelves. "Do you have *Not That He Brought Flowers?*" "Third shelf, poetry section. Left side, near the bottom. Behind the Gillian Clarke." He found it, crouching down with a slight lack of grace that he didn't seem to notice or perform. He pulled it out and stood, turning it in his hands with a kind of quiet attention that Rhiannon watched for a moment longer than she meant to. "You can sit, if you need to wait them out," she said, with the tone of someone making a practical concession rather than an invitation. "There's a chair by the window. It's got a cat on it, but she'll move." "What's the cat's name?" "Saunders." "After Saunders Lewis?" "After no one else." She allowed the smallest possible smile. "She's very nationalist. She'll judge you if you don't speak Welsh." "*Dw i'n dysgu,*" Maddox said, with an accent that was earnest and imperfect. Rhiannon stared at him. "You're learning Welsh." "I'm filming outside Abergavenny for six weeks. It seemed rude not to try." He paused. "That's probably the most impressive thing about me. More impressive than the films." "It is, actually." She said it before she'd decided to, and something crossed her face — a brief, involuntary candour. She looked back down at her book. "The chair's by the window." He took the Thomas collection with him. Saunders the cat regarded him with slow yellow eyes, then stood, stretched with magnificent indifference, and relocated to a shelf between Penelope Fitzgerald and some local history. The shop went quiet, except for the rain and the radiator. After perhaps ten minutes, Rhiannon looked up. He was reading — genuinely reading, one foot propped on the chair's edge, the book held close in the grey window light. He hadn't checked his phone. He hadn't looked at his reflection in the glass. He turned a page and said, without looking up, "The paparazzi have gone, by the way. You're not obliged to keep harbouring me." "I'm aware," she said. He looked up then, and she was already looking back at her book. Outside, the rain continued its quiet, indifferent work on the slate rooftops of Penmorfa, and neither of them moved to leave.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an assured, polished scene that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements with craft. The Welsh setting is authentically rendered through specific literary references — R.S. Thomas, Gillian Clarke, Saunders Lewis, a fictional town with slate rooftops, a nationalist cat, and a line of earnest, imperfect Welsh — rather than generic Welsh wallpapering. The actor-as-rogue-with-fragile-ego is established efficiently: the "smile" calibrated by a critic's quote, the drift toward people "that usually worked in his favour," the small self-deprecating bids for approval. Rhiannon's superficial immunity is done mostly through deflection and dry wit ("You're blocking the Welsh Poetry section"), and her involuntary candour — "It is, actually... before she'd decided to" — lands the inward flusterment with excellent restraint. The pivot on real, shared knowledge of R.S. Thomas derails the charm offensive believably; his genuine interest "arriving uninvited" is a nicely economical beat. Weaknesses are minor. The prompt requests "primarily in dialogue"; the piece is closer to half narration, though the narration is doing good show-don't-show work. The fragile ego could be prodded more — Rhiannon never really wounds him, so the "needs everyone to like him" trait is asserted more than tested. The paparazzi threat resolves off-stage rather tamely, and the ending, while lovely in its quiet stasis, borders on a familiar romantic-trope holding pattern (rain, radiator, neither moving to leave). "The rain continued its quiet, indifferent work" is a slight overreach toward the precious. Dialogue voices are distinct — his polished-then-genuine register versus her clipped, armoured dryness — and the rhythm between them is well controlled. Prose is clean, unshowy, with strong small images (the wheezing bell, ink on her finger, the cat relocating "with magnificent indifference"). No purple prose, no meandering, no unearned transformation: the mutual thaw is incremental and earned. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Morska Conspiracy ## Part III: The Underhold The door swung inward on silent hinges — too well-oiled, Aya noted, for a room supposedly left to rot and ruin. The smell hit her first: tallow candles, coal smoke, and beneath it something older. Brine and iron and age. The underhold was lit. A dozen lanterns burned in their brackets, casting the vaulted stone chamber in amber and shadow. The artifact — the *Scythan Coil*, that beautiful, terrible thing — sat untouched in its cradle at the room's far end, behind its lattice of warding-glass and iron chain. Between Aya and it stood Maren Voss, guild-mistress, decidedly unshackled, with four of her heaviest bodyguards arranged at her flanks like teeth in a jaw. Voss was a small woman, which had always been her most dangerous quality. She wore her silver hair pinned back with a stiletto. Her coat was good wool, her boots were better leather, and in her right hand she held a flintlock revolver with the casual authority of someone who had never once missed. "Close the door," she said pleasantly. Simeon's pocket watch ticked. Tick. Tick. Tick. Aya did not close the door. She did not move at all. Beside her she felt Katra go very still in the particular way that meant she was calculating distances, and Simeon's breathing had changed — shallow and fast, the sound a man made when he was doing arithmetic on his own mortality. *She was never arrested,* Aya thought, with the cold clarity that came to her in moments of genuine peril. *The raid was theatre. She drew us out.* "I said," Voss repeated, with the same pleasant tone, "close the door." One of the guards moved. Not toward the door — toward *Aya*. She had time to take one step backward before the hand closed on her collar, and then she was being walked forward into the room with her heels dragging against the stone, and she heard Katra's sharp intake of breath and Simeon's muttered *bloody hell* as the remaining guards swept in behind them. The door closed. Tick. Tick. Tick. The guard's hands found the edges of her mask — the thing she had worn every night for three years, the small dark mercy of anonymity — and tore it free. The cold air of the underhold touched her face. Voss looked at her for a long moment. Something moved behind those pale eyes. Not surprise. Never surprise. Recognition, perhaps, or the satisfaction of a theory confirmed. "Well," the guild-mistress said softly. "There it is." *They will know by morning.* The thought arrived with the mechanical certainty of a guillotine dropping. *Father will know. The whole of the Morska quarter will know. Lady Aya Vanthorpe, of the Vanthorpe banking house, playing thief in the dark — and worse. So much worse than thief.* Her mother's face surfaced, unbidden. The rope. The crowd. She made herself breathe. "Madame Voss," Aya said, and was quietly grateful that her voice came out level. "I see the evening's intelligence was somewhat selectively distributed." "I do find," Voss replied, "that a well-placed lie separates the ambitious from the merely greedy." She tilted her head. "You are ambitious, aren't you, girl. I've watched you for some time." "Then you'll know," Aya said, "that killing me would be a considerable waste." Katra made a small, pained sound. Aya did not look at her. "Is that a negotiation?" Voss sounded almost amused. "It's an observation." Aya kept her eyes on the guild-mistress and kept her hands very still at her sides. She could feel the immateria at the edges of her perception — that cold dark sea that her mother had taught her to swim before she'd learned to read — but she did not reach for it. Not yet. Not with four guns in the room and Simeon and Katra breathing beside her. "You have the Coil. You have the guild. You've demonstrated, this evening, that you have rather more control of the situation than any of us credited you with. What you don't have," she continued carefully, "is what I represent." Tick. Tick. Tick. "Which is?" Voss asked. "The Vanthorpe name. The Vanthorpe accounts." Aya let that sit for a moment in the lantern-light. "My father is not a sentimental man, but he is a practical one. He will pay a very great deal to avoid the particular scandal of his daughter's — extracurricular activities — becoming public record." "And if I simply make those activities *public*?" Voss said. "If I walk your unmasked face through the Morska quarter at dawn and let the broadsheets do the rest?" *Then I hang,* Aya thought. *As she did. In the same square, perhaps, if they want the poetry of it.* "Then you have a corpse," Aya said aloud, "and a dead hostage pays no ransom. Whereas a live one, properly handled, could fund your operation for the better part of a decade." She paused. "I am also," she added, with great deliberateness, "considerably more useful alive than dead in other respects. You know what I can do, Madame Voss. You've seen it." The silence stretched. Somewhere in the deep stone above them, the city breathed and groaned, its great brass machinery ticking over in the dark. Simeon's watch ticked. Voss lowered the revolver by perhaps two inches. Not a concession — a consideration. "Your friends," she said. "Are mine to vouch for." "That is not," Voss said gently, "what I asked." Aya looked at Katra then — Katra, who had followed her into every bad idea for seven years, whose dark eyes were steady and furious and frightened all at once. She looked at Simeon, pale beneath his collar, one hand pressed flat against his waistcoat over the watch as though he could muffle it. *I'm sorry,* she thought. *I'm so sorry.* "Name your terms," Aya said.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt with strong competence: the confrontation scene, capture, unmasking, and hostage negotiation all occur as specified, with no fight scene, third-person past tense, internal monologue, and heavy dialogue. The Victorian-gritty register is well maintained ("brass machinery ticking over in the dark," the flintlock revolver, broadsheets, banking houses), and the gothic undertone surfaces effectively in Aya's memory of her mother's hanging. Strengths: Voss is a genuinely menacing antagonist with a distinct voice — pleasant menace, economical lines. The ticking pocket watch is a nice recurring motif. Aya's negotiation is intelligent and in-character, and the internal monologue about her family discovering her identity is the emotional core, well rendered ("the mechanical certainty of a guillotine dropping"). The prose is controlled, with good rhythm and few wasted words. Weaknesses: The beats are handled somewhat efficiently rather than deeply — the capture happens very fast, and the guards are faceless furniture. Voss's "I've watched you for some time" is a familiar trope. The ending ("Name your terms") is a clean cliffhanger but the negotiation resolves a touch too smoothly; Voss's capitulation to conversation feels slightly under-pressured given her total dominance. Some phrases flirt with the ornamental ("teeth in a jaw," "small dark mercy of anonymity") but stay on the right side of purple. Katra and Simeon are thin — Simeon is essentially a ticking watch, Katra a pained sound. The mother's-rope callback is effective but brief; the piece could have earned more dread. Overall: a polished, atmospheric, professional scene that stops short of exceptional.
